blocks.text: It is proved that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as they hold, but a kind of larger mouse in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt and Libya, which is called Δίπους [Dipous] by Herodotus and others, Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios] by the Elders, Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys] by Jerome, and اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo by the Arabs; many things about it, not yet published, are brought forward from the writings of the Arabs.

In Levit, XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7., among those animals which do chew the cud but [col. 1002] do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean, השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan], is listed together with the camel and the hare. The plural שפנים sephanim occurs in Psal. CIV. 18.: The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And in Prov. XXX, 26.: שפנים sephanim, a feeble folk, make their house in the rock. Most of the more recent interpreters explain them as rabbits. Many things seem on the face of it to favour this interpretation. 1. That twice in the Law השפן is joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as a kindred animal. 2. That the passage of the Psalm which we have just cited is rendered thus in the Greek edition: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], The rock is a refuge for the hares. Some copies have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois], that is, as they hold, for the hedgehogs. But the most ancient writers follow the former reading. Jerome, Epistle 135, to Sunia and Fretela: All translated it with a similar word, χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious]; only the LXX rendered it hares. So too read Theodoret in his Commentary on this Psalm, Basil on Isaiah, chapter 2, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase:
Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ [Petrois ēlibatois peritharsees eisi lagōoi],

The hares trust in the sheer rocks; and the Arabic version, which was made from the Greek: The rock is the refuge الارانب [al-arānib] of the hares. Others join both: thus Augustine on this passage: The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs and the hares. Arnobius: There is the rock, affording a refuge either to the young of the hedgehogs, etc., or to the hares. Bede on Proverbs, chapter 30: And it is to be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing „The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs, in some manuscripts for the hares is found, in some for the choerogryllii“. 3. The Hebrew of Prov. XXX, 26., שפנים עם לא עצום, the Vulgate translator rendered thus: The little hare, a feeble folk, following, if I am not mistaken, [II, 410] some Greek translator who had explained שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, that is, rabbits. For thus in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, are taken for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For κόνιλος [konilos] in Aelian, κούνικλος [kouniklos] in Polybius and Galen, words of the Spaniards, and λεβηρὶς [lebēris] in Strabo and Erotian, a word of the Massilians, were local terms not used in Greece. 4. The old Book of Names, which they ascribe to Philo, has this under Jeremiah: SAPHAN, choerogryllius, hare, or hedgehog. And under Ezekiel: SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In Giggeius' Arabic Lexicon, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [safan] saphan is rendered cuniculus [rabbit]. Where he got this from, however, I do not know at all, for I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, of which the former means to cover, the latter to hide. And it seems to fit the rabbit, which seeks the hiding places of burrows, so as to lurk in them and be, as it were, covered over. Martial:
The rabbit delights to dwell in dug-out caves.
